message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Physical, Chemical, and Isotopic Properties**

| Property | Value / Description | Notes |
|----------|---------------------|-------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 | Only one proton in the nucleus. |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.00794 u (average) | Weighted average of its naturally occurring isotopes. |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ | One valence electron. |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 | Highest of all elements. |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) | Energy to remove the single valence electron. |
| **Electron affinity** | –0.754 eV (–72.8 kJ mol⁻¹) | Energy released when an electron is added. |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) | Extremely low; hydrogen is a gas at room temperature. |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) | Solidifies only at cryogenic temperatures. |
| **Density (at 0 °C, 1 atm)** | 0.08988 g cm⁻³ | Very light; less dense than air. |
| **Molar volume (ideal gas, 0 °C, 1 atm)** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ | Standard value for gases. |
| **State at room temperature** | Gas | Diatomic H₂ molecules. |
| **Molecular weight of H₂** | 2.01588 g mol⁻¹ | Two hydrogen atoms per molecule. |
| **Bond dissociation energy (H–H)** | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ | Energy required to break the H₂ bond. |
| **Dipole moment** | 0 D (non‑polar) | H₂ is a homonuclear diatomic molecule. |
| **Spectral lines** | Lyman, Balmer, Paschen series | Hydrogen’s emission/absorption lines are fundamental in astrophysics. |
| **Isotopes** |  |  |
| • **Protium (¹H)** | 99.98 % natural abundance | Single proton, no neutrons. |
| • **Deuterium (²H, D)** | 0.02 % natural abundance | One proton + one neutron. |
| • **Tritium (³H, T)** | Trace amounts | One proton + two neutrons; radioactive (half‑life ≈ 12.32 y). |
| **Chemical reactivity** | Highly reactive with many elements | Forms hydrides (e.g., NaH, CaH₂), acids (e.g., HCl, H₂SO₄), and organic compounds (e.g., alcohols, alkanes). |
| **Acidity/Basicity** | Weak acid in aqueous solution (pKa ≈ 15.7) | Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is a strong acid derived from hydrogen. |
| **Oxidation states** | +1 (most common), –1 (hydride), 0 (molecular H₂) | In compounds, hydrogen typically shows +1. |
| **Solubility in water** | 0.0006 g g⁻¹ at 25 °C | Very low; hydrogen is poorly soluble. |
| **Flammability** | Extremely flammable | Combustion produces water vapor: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O. |
| **Role in stars** | Fusion fuel | Proton–proton chain and CNO cycle convert hydrogen into helium, releasing energy. |
| **Applications** |  |  |
| • **Fuel** | Hydrogen fuel cells, rocket propellant | Clean energy source when produced from renewables. |
| • **Industrial** | Hydrogenation of fats, ammonia synthesis (Haber process) | Essential for many chemical processes. |
| • **Scientific** | Calibration gas, neutron sources (via deuterium) | Used in spectroscopy, neutron scattering, etc. |

### Quick Summary

- **Atomic & Molecular**: Hydrogen is the simplest element (1 proton, 1 electron) and exists as diatomic H₂ gas under normal conditions.
- **Physical**: Extremely low boiling/melting points, very low density, non‑polar molecule.
- **Chemical**: Highly reactive, forms hydrides, acids, and organic compounds; acts as a reducing agent.
- **Isotopic**: Protium (stable), Deuterium (stable, used in nuclear magnetic resonance), Tritium (radioactive, used in nuclear fusion research).
- **Astrophysical**: The most abundant element in the universe; fuels stellar fusion.
- **Technological**: Key component in fuel cells, industrial chemistry, and scientific instrumentation.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
